title: Inhibit Bands
subtitle: Reducing rewards when competing features appear
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical diagram illustrating inhibit bands within a neurofeedback closed loop.
learningObjectives: Explain inhibit bands without diagnostic overreach.
Distinguish measurement, mechanism and clinical outcome in inhibit bands.
Identify one safety or validity limitation relevant to inhibit bands.

sections.explainSimply: Inhibits can pause reward when slow activity, fast activity or artifact exceeds a criterion.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Inhibits may improve signal cleanliness or shape a broader state, but they increase protocol complexity and can reduce reward density.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: The rationale for every inhibit should be explicit. Multiple moving thresholds can make the actual contingency difficult to understand or reproduce.
sections.thinkOfItLike: A rehabilitation plan: define the target, dose, measurement and stopping rule before changing the exercise.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need to understand inhibit bands to evaluate mechanism claims, informed consent, treatment fit and whether change transfers to real-world function.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Too many inhibits can turn learning into unexplained failure.
sections.clinicalPearl: The trained metric is an intermediate target; the clinical endpoint is meaningful function.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician using inhibit bands predefines the target, checks raw signal and artifacts, monitors symptoms and function, and reviews whether change generalises beyond the feedback display.
sections.limitationsCautions: Too many inhibits can turn learning into unexplained failure. Evidence classification: practitioner convention; limited direct evidence.
